# Literature Review

## Crisis Informatics and Joint Triage Tasks

### Global Crisis Informatics

Disaster message classification consolidated early around a shared task formulation: given a crisis-related message, assign one humanitarian category. The CrisisNLP collections set the template [@imran2016twitter]: across 19 crises from 2013–2015, more than 52 million tweets were harvested in English, Spanish, and French, of which roughly 50,000 were annotated into the nine UN OCHA categories — injured or dead, missing or trapped, displaced and evacuations, infrastructure damage, donation needs or offers, caution and advice, sympathy, other useful, irrelevant — by volunteer and paid annotators. The modeling was shallow (naive Bayes, SVMs, random forests over n-gram features) and the reporting AUC-only, with per-class values spanning 0.23–0.97 on a single event; class imbalance was already the acknowledged obstacle. The corpus, not the models, was the contribution — and its nine-class inventory is the ancestor of most later label sets.

HumAID carried that lineage to its current benchmark form [@alam2021humaid]: 77,196 tweets sampled from 24.9 million across 19 events (2016–2019), annotated into eleven humanitarian categories by three-to-five crowd annotators per tweet (Fleiss' κ = 0.55), English-only by budget decision. Its transformer benchmarks fixed the reporting conventions this study inherits — F1-centric metrics over multiple seeded runs — and its ceiling: weighted F1 of 0.768 (BERT), 0.769 (DistilBERT), 0.777 (XLM-R), and 0.781 (RoBERTa) averaged over events, rising to 0.885 on the best single event. Notably, classes with fewer than 15 instances were removed before benchmarking — low-prevalence categories are dropped rather than solved.

A second thread made the task joint. On the TREC-IS corpus, @wang2021transformer learned two tasks from one corpus — twenty-five-type multi-label classification of information types, and priority estimation over four levels (critical, high, medium, low) cast as regression — with BERT-family encoders in a multi-task setup, evaluated on a held-out set of 2020 events. This event-level test split is the direct ancestor of this study's leave-one-disaster-out protocol, and its priority levels are the closest antecedent of the urgency axis; its headline result (NDCG ≈ 0.51 for the BERT multi-task model, with multi-task learning improving the alert-weighted metrics over single-task training) established that joint learning of type and priority is viable. @zahera2020iaid extended the multi-label formulation with structure: I-AID couples a BERT encoder with graph attention over word and named-entity nodes and a relation network, reaching weighted F1 0.59 on TREC-IS against 0.53 for the strongest baseline, while flagging class imbalance as unresolved. Entity recognition enters these systems as input features rather than as an evaluated span-level task.

The entity thread, and the strongest cross-event evidence, come from @seeberger2022enhancing: hierarchical multi-label classification over the TREC-IS label tree (four upper, twenty-five lower classes) trained with multi-task heads and entity-masked language modeling, evaluated on 21 held-out events (22,003 tweets) after training on 51 events (50,412 tweets). Span-level conventions appear here explicitly — entity masking over ten token types, validated at strict-match F1 0.692 on 300 manually annotated tweets — and macro-F1 on lower-level classes improved from 0.269 (BERT baseline) to 0.312, and on actionable types from 0.236 to 0.335. Their finding that event and regional differences degrade cross-event generalization is, in effect, the empirical case for this study's out-of-domain estimand.

The global record thus fixes conventions (per-class and macro F1, seeded runs, event-aware splits), ceilings (weighted F1 around 0.77–0.89 in-domain, in English), and the joint-task precedent — but it evaluates NER, intent, and priority separately or not at all, in English, in-domain or single-event splits, and without per-task interference accounting or efficiency measurement.

### Local Crisis Informatics (Philippines and Taglish)

The Philippine context adds an institutional and a linguistic layer. Institutionally, the disaster-response machinery that would consume triage output — councils, response pillars, situation reporting — is mandated by the Philippine DRRM Act of 2010 (RA 10121) and operationalized through NDRRMC situation reports. Scientifically, the foundational local evidence is @david2016tweeting: a content analysis of Twitter use during and after Typhoon Haiyan tracing how the platform's functions evolved across disaster phases. Its language finding anchors this study's roster design: during Haiyan — the most internationally salient Philippine disaster — tweets were 87% English against 11% Filipino, a composition that shifts toward Filipino in Luzon-centric events. Philippine disaster tweeting is reliably bilingual, with the balance set by event salience.

On the language-resource side, Taglish itself is under-instrumented. TweetTaglish [@herrera2022tweettaglish] remains the reference Taglish corpus: 21,150 tweets labeled word-by-word as English, Tagalog, or Other using a dictionary plus Tagalog-conjugation-rules identifier, yielding an average per-tweet composition of 55.2% Tagalog, 19.4% English, 24.5% Other — a Tagalog-dominant profile on average, with substantial per-tweet variance that is exactly what code-mixing strata partition. Its agreement evidence is thin (κ = 0.7 on a 20-tweet validation set), its downstream demonstration is share-prediction regression (R² 0.797–0.909), and its own search procedure was contaminated by Spanish cognates — a concrete illustration of the borrowing-and-cognate problem this study freezes as a pre-registered constant.

For named entity recognition, the local evidence is TF-NERD [@ramos2023tfnerd]: 2,337 paragraphs with 6,459 entity mentions over twelve OntoNotes-style types, drawn from Tagalog news, Wikipedia, and tweet sources, and fine-tuned on Tagalog-only encoders — reaching strict span F1 78.93 and boundary F1 87.14 with roberta-tagalog. Its evaluation discipline (four match regimes: strict, type-only, boundary-only, partial) prefigures this study's exact-match span convention. But it is single-annotator with no inter-annotator agreement reported, general-domain rather than disaster-focused, and does not quantify the code-mixing its own examples display.

What is missing locally is therefore precise: no Philippine corpus annotates the triage tasks jointly on a common Taglish corpus; no local benchmark reports code-mixing strata; nothing local evaluates under held-out events; and no local work profiles inference cost. The multitask code-mixed benchmark pattern does exist elsewhere — COMI-LINGUA [@sheth2025comilingua] annotates five tasks over 125,615 Hindi–English instances with per-task Fleiss' κ (average 0.863) and macro-F1 reporting — but for Hinglish, not Taglish. The gap this study fills is that pattern, imported to Philippine typhoon response: three tasks, one common corpus, Taglish strata, event-held-out evaluation.

## Taglish Code-Mixing, Low-Resource NLP, and the SEA-LION Encoder

Taglish is difficult for subword models for structural reasons before statistical ones. In the matrix language frame [@myersscotton1993duelling], code-switched discourse pairs a matrix language — the one supplying the morphosyntactic frame — with embedded-language insertions [@muysken1995review]; Taglish is typically Tagalog-framed with English content morphemes. Two consequences follow. First, a tweet's difficulty is not captured by its "percentage of English" but by which language supplies the frame and how the other is threaded through it. Second, the measurement primitive is word-level language identification — itself the hard case of LID — the last language identification frontier [@das2013codemixing] — precisely because code-mixed social media text breaks the one-text-one-language assumption the tooling was built on.

The study therefore freezes an explicit mixing measure: the utterance-level code-mixing index of @gamback2016comparing. With $N(x)$ the number of language-dependent tokens in tweet $x$ and $t_L(x)$ the count assigned to language $L$, the index is $C_u(x) = \big(N(x) - \max_{L}\, t_L(x)\big) / N(x)$, reported as a percentage — in words, the share of a message's language-dependent tokens that fall outside its matrix language, where the matrix language is the utterance's most frequent language and language-independent tokens are excluded from $N(x)$ entirely. Three properties justify the freeze. It is matrix-relative, matching exactly what the study's strata mean (Tagalog-dominant, Mixed, English-dominant name the matrix language and the degree of mixing). It is utterance-level, and the unit of analysis is the tweet; the same paper's corpus-level construct — which weights code-alternation points and switched-utterance shares, yielding for instance a corpus CMI of 21.97 for an English–Spanish Twitter corpus — serves cross-corpus comparison, not per-tweet assignment. And it is computable from word-level labels of the TweetTaglish kind [@herrera2022tweettaglish], the labeling convention already used for Taglish, with Hinglish benchmarks reporting mean CMI 18.96 across five annotated tasks [@sheth2025comilingua] as the comparator class. The borrowing and cognate treatment — whether a borrowed token counts as matrix, embedded, or language-independent — is frozen together with the stratum thresholds before annotation begins: it changes $N(x)$ and the maximum simultaneously, and TweetTaglish's Spanish-cognate query contamination is the standing example of what an unmade decision costs.

Tokenizer fertility — subwords per word — is the explanatory variable for how unevenly one vocabulary serves two languages. English-centric vocabularies tax other languages measurably: on commercial tokenizers, some mid-resourced languages pay up to roughly five times English's token count for the same text [@ahia2023tokenization]. Latin-script Tagalog sits on the cheaper end of that spectrum and no Tagalog-specific premium is reported — which is why this study measures fertility per stratum on its own corpus rather than importing a number, with the launch checklist's fertility probe (at least 500 sampled tweets per stratum, the SEA-LION tokenizer against one multilingual baseline) quantifying the cost before commitment. The tokenization-free escape — character-level encoders [@clark2022canine] — trades vocabulary bias for roughly fourfold longer sequences under quadratic attention and offers no competitive Tagalog-pretrained checkpoint; the study stays subword and audits fertility instead of assuming it.

The encoder decision weighs architecture generation, language coverage, and terms. ModernBERT [@warner2025modernbert] modernized the bidirectional encoder for speed, memory efficiency, and long context (8,192 tokens). AI Singapore pretrained a from-scratch ModernBERT-base for the region: SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M [@aisingapore2026sealion] — 22 layers, hidden size 768, Gemma-3 SentencePiece vocabulary of 262,144 — over two pretraining phases totaling three trillion tokens across thirteen languages plus code, with Filipino holding a dedicated 2.5% token share and English 35%. It is MIT-licensed, requires `transformers` ≥ 4.48, and is evaluated across the SEA-BED suite (169 datasets, ten Southeast Asian languages including Filipino), CMTEB, and MTEB per its model card. The English-heavy, Filipino-light mix is not a defect the study conceals but the stated reason for two design choices: the stratified hypothesis exists because transfer may differ by language balance, and multitask supervision is the low-resource regularizer operating on exactly this distribution. Monolingual Tagalog encoders (§2.1's TF-NERD baselines) cannot carry the embedded English half of Taglish — the encoder needs both languages in one vocabulary.

The comparison set is the standard one. mBERT [@devlin2019bert] is the 2019-era default: pretrained over the 104 largest Wikipedias including Filipino, roughly 177M parameters over a shared WordPiece vocabulary of about 110K entries. DistilmBERT [@sanh2019distilbert] is its six-layer, 134M-parameter distillation at about twice the speed, inheriting the same vocabulary and coverage. XLM-R base [@conneau2020xlmr] is the strongest general multilingual encoder: 278.9M parameters, a 250K-entry SentencePiece vocabulary trained on filtered CommonCrawl across 100 languages including Tagalog, MIT-licensed — but of the previous architecture generation. Only the SEA-LION encoder combines dedicated Filipino pretraining, modern-architecture efficiency, a permissive license, and current tooling; @tbl-encoders states the full matrix.

| Filipino pretraining | Dedicated 2.5% token share; 13 SEA languages plus code; 3T tokens, two phases | One of 104 Wikipedia languages; no dedicated share | Inherits mBERT coverage via distillation | One of 100 CC100 languages; no per-language share stated |

## Multi-Task Optimization and Balancing

Hard parameter sharing creates one optimization problem out of $T$ tasks: one shared parameter vector, one update direction per step, $T$ loss surfaces pulling on it. Balancing methods are the mechanisms that decide each task's influence on that direction, and they come in two families. Loss-space methods weight the losses — static scalarization, $\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \sum_{t=1}^{T} w_t\, \mathcal{L}_t(\theta)$ — with uniform weighting ($w_t = 1$ for all tasks) at one end and tuned static weights, searched before or within training, at the other; on mean-reduced losses, uniform 1:1:1 weighting is scale-comparable across tasks, which is what makes it a meaningful baseline rather than an arbitrary one. Gradient-space methods alter the per-task gradients before they combine. The multi-objective formulation of @sener2018multitask treats MTL as Pareto optimization — the update is the minimum-norm point of the tasks' gradient convex hull — at a measured price: explicit per-task gradients mean $T$ backward passes per step, linearly multiplying training time (their upper-bound variant recovers a single backward pass through representation gradients, with most of the savings: 38.6 h to 23.3 h on their scene-understanding suite).

The canonical gradient-space method is PCGrad [@yu2020gradient]: when two task gradients conflict — their cosine is negative — each is projected onto the normal plane of the other, removing exactly the component along which they oppose:

$$g_i \;\leftarrow\; g_i \;-\; \frac{g_i^{\top} g_j}{\lVert g_j \rVert^{2}}\, g_j \qquad \text{if } \cos(g_i, g_j) < 0$$ {#eq-pcgrad}

iterated over task pairs in random order, with the final update the sum of projected gradients. Its cost is structural: per-task backward passes to obtain the gradients, plus storage for $T$ gradient vectors — in PCGrad's own supervised experiments, convergence time grew from 8 to 12 hours and peak GPU memory from 6 to 10 GB, and later timing measurements put its per-step cost at 9.7–59.8 s on ten- and fifty-task reinforcement learning suites [@liu2021cagrad]. Its guarantees are modest: convergence is proven only for two-task convex problems, and at $\cos = -1$ the projection zeroes the update entirely. CAGrad [@liu2021cagrad] is the bounded-deviation alternative — optimize the worst-case task improvement within a neighborhood of the average gradient — with faster task-subsampling variants; it belongs here as context for the design space, not as a studied arm.

The critical record is what the study's hypotheses lean on, and it converges from four directions. PCGrad's own authors characterize its supervised gains as "a regularization effect, rather than an improvement on optimization speed or convergence" [@yu2020gradient]. @xin2022current audited the field at scale and found that, despite their design and computational complexity, MTO methods "do not yield any performance improvements beyond what is achievable via traditional optimization approaches," with common training pitfalls and benchmarking fragility explaining much of the reported advantage. @kurin2022defense went further: unitary scalarization — minimizing the plain sum of losses — equipped with standard regularization and stabilization matches or beats complex per-task-gradient optimizers, and many specialized optimizers are interpretable as implicit regularization. @gama2025uniform extended the debate under grid-searched hyperparameters across fourteen specialized methods: gaps are domain-dependent, static weights derived from optimizer behavior nearly match the specialists, several methods provably reduce to equal weighting under symmetric conditions — and, decisively for this study's diagnostics, their measured mean gradient cosines sit around 0.7 in simple settings and 0.3–0.45 in complex ones: task gradients are mostly far from head-on conflict, so destructive conflict is a tail event, not the regime. @jiang2023forkmerge complete the reversal: negative transfer is routinely blamed on gradient conflict, but optimization-based coordination "largely overlooks the auxiliary-target generalization capability" — ForkMerge attacks transfer through periodic forking, weight search, and merging rather than through the gradients at all.

This record dictates the study's arm set. Uniform scalarization is the baseline the critical literature rehabilitated; tuned static scalarization is the control that kills the tuning-budget confound @xin2022current identified; PCGrad is the dynamic representative — the simplest surgery, implementable side-effect-free, and the only method whose trigger *is* the conflict measure the diagnostics log, so method and instrument share one cosine. The design internalizes the record's central lesson as budget parity: identical hyperparameter grids and budgets for every arm, so the comparison isolates the balancing mechanism and not the search behind it.

Balancing is a training-time concern; at inference the efficiency question is purely architectural — one shared encoder with three heads resident, or three single-task encoders resident — and the footprint arithmetic is dominated by the embedding matrix (§3.8's two-thirds note). The published efficiency levers are background, not tested claims here: distillation (DistilBERT: 40% smaller, 60% faster, retaining 97% of BERT's performance [@sanh2019distilbert]) and efficiency-first architecture design [@warner2025modernbert]. Published latency and memory figures come from heterogeneous hardware, precision, and workload assumptions, so this study measures its own serving configurations under the frozen instrument rules of the Methodology — commodity machine, frozen precision and power mode, batch-1 all-tasks workload — and makes no claim about edge deployments it does not profile.
